one-check-per-line.why: all 2 lines quoted in order, checks numbered 1 to 2

no-restated-rules.why: no branch, base, branch-name rule or return mechanics named

builder-criteria.why: all 2 lines quoted in the builder brief

words-only.why: I compared each check's PASS and FAIL conditions with the words of its expect line. Check 1 passes when the call on invalid JSON "does not throw, the printed result is `RESULT {}`" and loadConfig in src/config.js catches the JSON.parse error. It fails on a throw, a result other than {}, or catching that happens somewhere other than loadConfig. The expect line's words ask for each of these things. Check 2 passes when npm test "exits successfully and reports no failing tests" and fails otherwise, which is what "npm test passes" means. The stricter items all sit under "Advisory (not PASS or FAIL conditions)": valid JSON still parsing, a missing path still throwing, the stderr warning, the README update and replacing the old test. Neither check's PASS or FAIL condition adds a mutation test, a branch or file-scope rule, or an exact-wording rule.

runs-as-written.why: Most commands hold up. `npm test` maps to `node --test`. The verifier's `printf … && node --input-type=module -e "import { loadConfig } from './src/config.js' …"` is valid shell and JS, and the import resolves from the repository root. Its `printf` commands for the good and bad config files are also fine. One advisory command breaks the criterion: `node src/app.js /tmp/bad-config.json`. Nothing the brief stage reported shows that src/app.js reads a config path from argv. The builder brief describes the failure only as "exiting 1 on a bad config.json", which points to a fixed config.json file rather than a command-line argument. The verifier brief's own wording, "now probably starts on defaults", shows the command wasn't checked against the program. So that argument isn't shown to fit app.js, and if the app starts a server the command may never exit. Not every command is shown to run as written.

catches-traps.why:
I checked all three must_catch items, and the briefs handle each one.

1. The hidden-file trap is flagged outside the PASS/FAIL conditions in two places. The builder brief says "Returning `{}` with no message would hide that" and "src/app.js no longer reaches its catch for bad JSON; the app starts with DEFAULTS". The second line is where app.js prints 'bad config'. The verifier's Advisory section also notes that the app "now probably starts on defaults instead of exiting 1".
2. Builder step 3 says to replace 'bad JSON throws' with a test that expects `{}`. The brief's current-state section explains why: that test "contradicts line 1 and has to change". Step 5 then requires `npm test` to pass.
3. Verifier Check 1 writes `{port: 9000` to a file and calls loadConfig on it. It PASSes only if the call doesn't throw and prints `RESULT {}`.

avoids-must-not.why: The verifier brief is fine on must_not item 1. Check 1 passes only when the call returns `RESULT {}` and the catch is in loadConfig. The stderr warning appears only under "Advisory (not PASS or FAIL conditions)". The builder brief breaks item 2. Step 2 requires extra behavior on a parse error: "Inside the catch, before returning `{}`, write a one-line warning to stderr ... that names `path` and includes the parse error's message." Step 6 repeats it for the PR description. Item 1 of the must_not list names "logging a warning" as asking for more than returning {}. So requiring a warning means the builder does more than just return {}. The brief also claims "This does not conflict with line 1". It still adds behavior the issue's line 1 doesn't ask for.

methods-private.why: I checked the builder brief for any PASS/FAIL condition or probe that also appears in the verifier brief. Most of it is allowed: step 1 restates expect line 1, and step 5 tells the builder to run `npm test`, which the issue names. The problem is step 3. It tells the builder to assert `loadConfig(file('{port: 9000'))` deep-equals `{}`. That is the same input and expected output as the verifier's Check 1 probe, which writes `printf '{port: 9000'` to a file and passes only if the result is `RESULT {}`. Writing its own tests is allowed, but here the brief dictates the exact assertion the checker will use, so the builder receives the checker's method. The input comes from the repo's existing test, but under a strict reading the criterion still breaks on this overlap.
